Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- 3-day history of profuse watery→loose diarrhoea (≥4 episodes today), repeated vomiting, subjective fever, and periumbilical abdominal pain. Brother has identical illness, suggesting contagious gastroenteritis.  
- No red-flag features of GI bleed; passing urine within last hour indicates some hydration, but ongoing emesis raises risk of dehydration.  
- Most likely diagnosis: acute infectious gastroenteritis, probably viral (norovirus) but bacterial cause cannot be excluded given persistence, reported high fever, and abdominal pain.  
- Plan:  
  • Urgent face-to-face clinic appointment for examination of hydration status and abdominal findings.  
  • Provide stool sample at clinic for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity.  
  • Continue oral rehydration solution (ORS) with very small, frequent sips.  
  • Dietary advice: bland foods (toast, biscuits); avoid dairy, fruit, high-fiber vegetables.  
  • Safety-net: attend Emergency Department if unable to keep fluids down, reduced urine output, worsening abdominal pain, bloody stools, or escalating fever.  
  • No routine antibiotics at this stage; decision pending stool results and clinical review.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus) – High likelihood: sudden onset, household cluster, watery diarrhoea + vomiting, no blood.  
2. Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (Campylobacter/Salmonella/E. coli) – Moderate likelihood: persistent symptoms >72 h and subjective fever; stool culture warranted.  
3. Food-borne toxin–mediated illness – Low–moderate likelihood: prominent vomiting early, but duration >24 h makes this less likely.
